c:count_status_t.why: the counted-event payload. rmw declares one status struct per event (`rmw_requested_deadline_missed_status_t`, `rmw_offered_deadline_missed_status_t`, `rmw_message_lost_status_t`) that are field-identical, and rclcpp typedefs each one to its own `QOS*Info` name. Ours is a single `nros_count_status_t` (`total_count`, `total_count_change`) shared by all three, plus `nros_liveliness_changed_status_t` for the one that differs. The widths are fixed (`uint32_t`, and `uint16_t`/`int16_t` for the liveliness counters) rather than `size_t`/`int32_t`: the payload crosses the C ABI BY VALUE into a callback, so it must have one layout on a 64-bit host and a 32-bit target -- the same hand-mirrored-FFI-struct hazard issue 0160 gated. These print as ours-only because the ROS 2 originals live in `rmw`, which is outside the rclc+rcl surface this report compares.

c:event_fini.why: rcl makes a QoS event a first-class OBJECT: `rcl_event_t` is initialised from an entity plus an event-type enum, added to a wait set, and drained with `rcl_take_event`. Ours registers a typed callback per event directly on the entity, so there is no event handle to zero-initialise, validate, add to a set or finalise. Constraints: no allocator for the `rcl_event_impl_t` the handle hides, and RFC-0002's executor drives entities through the RMW vtable with no wait set for an event to join. Same decision the pubsub stage recorded for the callbacks themselves -- see `cpp:QOSEventHandler`.

c:node_set_qos_overrides.why: installs the baked override table on the node, once, before any entity is created. The ours-only half of `cpp:QosOverridingOptions`; the same call exists in all three languages under the same name (`nros_node_set_qos_overrides`, `Node::set_qos_overrides`, `NodeHandle::set_qos_overrides`), which is the one place this stage found our languages already agreeing. QoS overrides. rclcpp's `QosOverridingOptions` is handed to each entity's options at creation; it DECLARES `qos_overrides.<topic>.<role>.<policy>` parameters on the node, reads them back at runtime and runs a user validation callback over the result. Ours keeps the same launch-parameter spelling but resolves it at BUILD time: the deploy plan lowers each override into a `&'static [QoSOverride]` table, the entry installs it once with `set_qos_overrides` before any entity exists, and the node folds the matching `(topic, role)` rows into the profile inside `create_publisher`/`create_subscription` -- setup-time, before the backend-compat check, so there is still no silent downgrade. Constraints: no allocator for a per-entity options object, and QoS is a compile-time selection (RFC-0036/0045) so there is no runtime parameter machinery in the create path to read a value out of. A user loses re-tuning QoS by editing a YAML on the device; they re-run the plan instead.

c:qos_durability_t.why: the ROS 2 counterpart is `rmw_qos_profile_t` / `rmw_qos_*_policy_t`, declared in `rmw` and only re-exported by rcl, so it prints ours-only against the rclc+rcl surface this report compares. `nros_qos_t` matches the field set. Two substantive differences: our policy enums carry no `SYSTEM_DEFAULT` and no `UNKNOWN` discriminant (RFC-0036 selects QoS at COMPILE time against a backend linked at build time -- there is no middleware to defer to and no remote endpoint to read an unknown value off), and the three time windows are `uint32_t` milliseconds rather than `rmw_time_t`. CORRECTED 2026-08-27 (phase-379 W5): that last clause used to read "because neither C nor C++ has a duration type here (timer stage, `cpp:Duration::Duration`)", and every part of it is dead. C has `nros_duration_t` / `nros_duration_from_nanoseconds` (ledgered as `c:duration_value_t`), C++ has `nros::Duration` since 2026-08-25 (issue 0789), Rust has both `Duration` and `TimerDuration`, and `cpp:Duration::Duration` names a key that exists in no shard. The millisecond unit is a DECISION about this shared repr(C) record -- one 4-byte field per window instead of `rmw_time_t`'s 16, on a part where the QoS table is static storage -- not a consequence of a type nobody had. The C++ accessors now take and return `nros::Duration` and convert at this boundary (`cpp:QoS::deadline_ms` records the rounding rule); the C ABI did not move.

cpp:ClockQoS.why: the clock preset (best-effort, keep-last(1)). OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: our C++ ships exactly THREE QoS presets -- `QoS::default_profile()`, `QoS::sensor_data()`, `QoS::services()` (qos.hpp) -- and C ships the same three as constants (`NROS_QOS_DEFAULT`, `NROS_QOS_SENSOR_DATA`, `NROS_QOS_SERVICES`), while Rust's `QoSProfile` ships twelve: topics, sensor_data, services, parameters, parameter_events, clock, action_status, system, px4, plus the BEST_EFFORT/RELIABLE consts. So the profiles our OWN Rust parameter, clock and action code publishes on are unspellable from C and C++, and a ported node has to open a DDS reference and retype the numbers. Not a divergence -- nothing about a device stops a `constexpr QoS` named constructor from existing; the presets are just values. Phase 379 W3. cpp:QOSOfferedIncompatibleQoSCallbackTyp.why: the incompatible-QoS event fires when DISCOVERY finds a remote endpoint whose offered profile does not match the requested one. cpp:QoSCheckCompatibleResult.why: RxO compatibility between a publisher profile and a subscription profile. Answering it needs the REMOTE endpoint's offered QoS, which arrives through discovery; we have static peers and no dynamic discovery, so there is no second profile to compare against. What we check instead is a different question with the same name-shape: `QoSProfile::validate_against(Session::supported_qos_policies())` compares the requested profile with what the LINKED BACKEND can honour and makes the create call return `INCOMPATIBLE_QOS` (RFC-0036, no silent downgrade). `QoSCheckCompatibleResult` additionally carries a `std::string reason`, which the freestanding build has no allocator for, and `qos_check_compatible` reports failure by throwing `QoSCheckCompatibilityException` (-fno-exceptions, RFC-0018). A user loses the "will these two endpoints talk?" pre-flight; they get a create-time error instead. rust:QoSOverride.why: ROS 2 implements `qos_overrides.<topic>.<role>.<policy>` launch parameters through the PARAMETER system at runtime: rclcpp's `QosOverridingOptions` declares them on the node and rebuilds the entity's profile from the declared values. Nothing here can do that -- entity QoS is compile-time (RFC-0036/0045) and there is no runtime parameter callback to rebuild an entity from. So the planner lowers the same launch parameter into a baked `&'static [QoSOverride]` table and the entity folds the matching rows in at create time: one linear scan, no alloc, before the backend-compat check, so an override the active RMW cannot honour still errors loudly. rclrs has no QoS-override support at all.

rust:QoSOverrideRole.why: which side of the topic an override targets -- the `<role>` segment of `qos_overrides.<topic>.<role>.<policy>`. See `rust:QoSOverride`.

rust:QoSOverrideValue.why: one typed policy+value an override sets. A typed enum rather than a string so codegen catches an unknown policy at BAKE time instead of silently no-op-ing on target. See `rust:QoSOverride`.

rust:QoSPolicyMask.why: the bitset those two exchange -- one bit per policy a backend either can or cannot honour. See `rust:QoSProfile::required_policies`.

rust:QoSProfile::apply_override_codes.why: the same fold over the primitive wire form a baked table travels in (issue 0303), which is what the C and C++ ABIs carry. See `rust:QoSOverride`.

rust:QoSProfile::apply_override_value.why: the ONE place a policy maps to the field it sets, so a new policy cannot reach some paths only. See `rust:QoSOverride`.

rust:QoSProfile::apply_overrides.why: the fold itself, at `create_publisher`/`create_subscription` time. See `rust:QoSOverride`.

rust:QoSProfile::depth.why: enum-taking chainable setters. rclrs's `QoSProfile` offers only the policy-specific shorthands (`reliable()`, `best_effort()`, `keep_last(n)`, ...) and rclcpp's `QoS` has the enum-taking form; ours has BOTH, which is why these four are unmatched while the shorthands beside them are renames. They exist because codegen bakes a profile from a plan and needs to set one policy from a value rather than from a method name -- our own `QoSProfile::apply_override_value` is the caller. Note our C++ `nros::QoS` does NOT have them, so this is Rust-only among our three languages. All four are `const fn`, so the profile is still buildable in a `static`.

rust:QoSProfile::history_depth.why: `depth` narrowed to the `uint8_t` the C ABI and the backend handle tables carry, saturating at 255. rclrs keeps one `u32` because rcl takes a `size_t`; ours needs the narrowed read because the value crosses a `repr(C)` boundary into a fixed-width field. The doc comment says "for backwards compatibility", which is not a reason -- worth a look in W5.

rust:QoSProfile::new.why: a `const fn` returning `QOS_PROFILE_DEFAULT`, so a profile can be built in a `static` / `const` initialiser. That is what compile-time QoS (RFC-0036/0045) needs: the entity's profile is baked, not assembled at runtime. rclrs builds a `QoSProfile` through the `*_default()` constructors or `Default`.

rust:QoSProfile::px4.why: the QoS PX4's `uxrce_dds_client` uses on `/fmu/out/*` and `/fmu/in/*` -- BEST_EFFORT + VOLATILE + KEEP_LAST(1). A companion-computer node talking to the same `MicroXRCEAgent` must match it exactly or nothing is delivered (verified against PX4 SITL: a TRANSIENT_LOCAL reader silently fails to match `/fmu/out/*`). RFC-0039 Track B. rclrs has no vendor profiles because a desktop node discovers and negotiates instead.

rust:QoSProfile::required_policies.why: backend-compatibility validation. Backends differ in which QoS policies they can honour at all -- zenoh-pico enforces no DEADLINE or LIFESPAN, XRCE none of the extended set -- so an entity requesting one the active backend cannot keep fails SYNCHRONOUSLY at create time with `TransportError::IncompatibleQos`, never a silent downgrade. ROS 2 answers the same question at runtime instead, through RxO matching and a QOS_INCOMPATIBLE event on the entity; both halves of that need dynamic discovery and the QoS event surface, and we have neither (see the qos stage's `c:get_zero_initialized_event`). `required_policies` reports what a profile asks for, `validate_against` checks it against what the session advertises.

rust:QoSProfile::tx_express.why: publisher-side batching-bypass hint (phase-279, issue 0145): this publisher's samples set zenoh's wire EXPRESS flag, so a batching zenoh-pico session sends them immediately instead of queueing them for the next flush. A TRANSPORT hint, not a DDS policy -- no RxO matching, no backend-compat validation, ignored by subscriptions and by backends with no batching concept. It exists because a control-tier topic on a slow serial link pays the batch window in latency, which is not a problem a desktop RMW has. Our C++ `nros::QoS` has the same setter.

rust:Session::next_deadline_ms.why: the backend's own next internal deadline (lease keepalive, heartbeat, ACK-NACK timeout), so the executor can cap its wait against it instead of waking early on a quiet link and round-tripping back into `drive_io`. See `rust:Session`.

rust:Session::supported_qos_policies.why: the RMW SEAM, one layer below the user API -- what a backend implements, not what a node calls; see `rust:Session::create_publisher` in the pubsub stage, and issue 0784 on `nros::` exporting the seam beside the API. rclrs has no equivalent because rcl is its only backend and DDS is assumed to honour every policy. It exists here because ours do not: zenoh-pico honours a different subset from Cyclone, and `QoSProfile::validate_against` uses this mask to fail a create call with `INCOMPATIBLE_QOS` rather than downgrade silently (RFC-0036). OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: this is the only way in any of our three languages to ask which policies the linked backend honours, and it is Rust-only -- a C or C++ caller learns the answer only by getting `NROS_RET_INCOMPATIBLE_QOS` back from a create it already made. Same asymmetry as `Publisher::supports_event` in the pubsub stage.

rust:QoSProfile::resolve_system_default.why: issue 0829. Replaces each `SYSTEM_DEFAULT` field with the backend's own answer, and is called by every backend at its create entry. rclrs has no counterpart because upstream never resolves the sentinel in the client library: `rmw_qos_profile_system_default` is passed down untouched and each `librmw_*_cpp.so` resolves it internally, differently -- `rmw_cyclonedds_cpp`'s `create_readwrite_qos` gives `KEEP_LAST, 1`, `rmw_zenoh_cpp`'s `QoS::QoS()` gives `RMW_ZENOH_DEFAULT_HISTORY_DEPTH` (42). We link ONE backend at build time and our backends are Rust crates implementing `nros_rmw::Session` from other crates, so the same per-backend resolution has to be a public item on the shared `QoSProfile` rather than private C++ inside a dynamically-loaded plugin. One shared helper, not three spellings.

rust:QoSProfile::has_unresolved_system_d.why: issue 0829. Predicate for `is any policy field still the sentinel`, the guard a backend or test uses to assert resolution happened before anything is derived from the profile -- load-bearing on the zenoh path, where the QoS is serialised into a liveliness-token keyexpr that a ROS `rmw_zenoh_cpp` peer parses, and an unresolved `0:0:0,0` would advertise a policy nobody chose. rclrs exposes nothing equivalent for the same reason as `resolve_system_default`: upstream's resolution is invisible C++ inside the loaded RMW, so there is no client-library state to ask about.

They are `= delete` overloads now, sharing one diagnostic -- a refusal is per-CONCEPT, not per-symbol.
